records.source_text:
Exercise 6.6 — Monotone safe-state set and the fail set
      
      
        Prove Lemma A.16, $X^s_n\subseteq X^s_{n+1}$, from the monotonicity of $l_n$ and $\mathcal B_n$. Then explain why GoSafeOpt re-checks the states in $X_{\rm Fail}$ after every LSE phase and what would be lost if failed parameters stayed in $E$ forever.
        
          Show answer
          
            Take $x\in X^s_n$: some $(a',x')\in\mathcal B_n$ satisfies $\|x'-x\|\le\frac1{L_x}\min_i l_n(a',i)-\Xi$. Backups are never removed, so $(a',x')\in\mathcal B_{n+1}$, and lower bounds are updated by $l_{n+1}=\max\{l_n,\mu_n-\beta_{n+1}\sigma_n\}\ge l_n$ (or by intersection with $[0,\infty)$ after a successful GE step), so $\min_il_{n+1}(a',i)\ge\min_il_n(a',i)$ and the same pair certifies $x$ at $n+1$. Hence $X^s_n\subseteq X^s_{n+1}$.
            A GE experiment interrupted at $x_{\rm Fail}$ was interrupted because $x_{\rm Fail}\notin X^s_n$ at that time, not because the parameter is unsafe. After LSE in a new region, $\mathcal B_n$ contains states from new trajectories and the bounds have tightened, so $X^s_n$ may now contain $x_{\rm Fail}$; Algorithm 4 then removes the parameter from $E$ so that eq. 11 can propose it again. Keeping it in $E$ forever would make the acquisition ignore parameters that have become certifiable, and the discoverability argument of Lemma A.17, which needs every parameter whose trajectory lies in $X^s_n$ to be eventually tried, would fail: the optimum could be permanently locked out by an early, premature interruption.
